desc:
Two numbers are bit-disjoint when their bitwise AND (&) is 0, meaning they never have a 1 bit in the same position.

Choose two different indices i != j whose values are bit-disjoint and maximise nums[i] * nums[j]. Return that maximum product, or 0 if no such pair exists.

nums = [1, 2, 4, 8]   -> 32   (4 and 8)
nums = [2, 4, 8, 3]   -> 32   (4 and 8)
nums = [3, 5, 7]      -> 0    (every pair shares a bit)
hints: Checking all pairs takes quadratic time, which is too slow for 5,000 numbers. For a value x, which values are bit-disjoint with it?
A value is disjoint from x exactly when it is a submask of the complement 4095 ^ x. So let best[m] be the largest present value that is a submask of m; the best partner for x is best[4095 ^ x].
Compute best with the subset-sum (SOS) dynamic programme: for each bit b, every mask containing b takes the maximum of its own value and the value of the mask with b removed.
editorial: Values fit in 12 bits, so let FULL = 4095. For any value x, the bit-disjoint values are exactly the submasks of FULL ^ x. Since the product grows with each factor, for a fixed x the best partner is the largest submask value present.

Build best[m], the largest present value that is a submask of m, for all 4096 masks with the SOS DP: initialise best[v] = v for present values, then for each bit b and each mask m with bit b set, update best[m] = max(best[m], best[m without b]). Then scan the distinct values. The DP costs 12 * 4096 steps and the scan is linear in the input.
Zero is disjoint with everything, but it only gives products of 0, which is the default answer. Two equal values are never disjoint unless both are 0, so working with the distinct values is enough.
